enrichment.short_title: Conditions on appeal where foreign judgment debtor refuses to pay
key_facts: Langley J ordered Taiwanese mobility-scooter manufacturer Pihsiang and its directors to pay distributor Days Medical Aids about £10.2m plus £2m interim costs after breach of a distributorship agreement.
The defendants refused to pay the judgment or interim costs and their stay application was refused, with parent company DCC offering a repayment guarantee.
On permission to appeal, the claimants sought conditions requiring payment of the full judgment debt, interim costs, and £150,000 security for appeal costs.
Enforcement in Taiwan would require recognition proceedings taking years and could not begin while the English appeal remained pending.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to impose conditions on permission to appeal an adjourned issue following grant of permission in principle.
enrichment.outcome: Conditions imposed requiring payment of the judgment sum plus interest, £2m interim costs plus interest, and £150,000 security for costs within six weeks; defendants to pay the costs of the application.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 52.3 and 52.9, conditions on permission to appeal may be imposed only where there is a compelling reason; where an appellant in deliberate breach of payment orders, with means to pay, has been refused a stay, and faces practical foreign enforcement difficulties, compelling reasons exist to require payment of the judgment debt and costs as a condition of proceeding, and any Article 14 discrimination against foreign-resident defendants is objectively justified.
legal_issues: Whether permission to appeal should be subject to payment of the full judgment debt and interim costs
Whether there was a compelling reason to impose such conditions under CPR 52.9
Whether imposing conditions would breach Article 14 ECHR by discriminating against foreign-resident defendants
What amount of security for costs was appropriate
linked_authorities: Hammond Suddards Solicitors v Agrichem International Holdings Ltd [2002] CP Rep 21
Bell Electric Ltd v Aweco Appliance Systems GmbH & Co KG [2003] 1 All ER 344
Fitzgerald v Williams [1996] QB 657

confidence.notes: Outcome, CPR provisions, and conditions ordered are explicit. Merits of the underlying appeal were not considered.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of disabled badge parking penalty in residents' bay

statutes_considered.title: Local Authorities Traffic Orders (Exemptions for Disabled Persons) (England) Regulations 2000

key_facts: Mr Welsh received a penalty charge notice for parking in a Watford residents' permit bay while displaying a disabled Blue Badge but no residents' permit.
A parking adjudicator dismissed his appeal, holding Blue Badge holders could not use residents' bays without a permit or visitor voucher.
Mr Welsh sought judicial review both of the adjudicator's decision and of the underlying traffic regulation order, long after the relevant time limits.
He argued the scheme discriminated against disabled persons and that adjudicator procedures breached Articles 6 and 14 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of a parking adjudicator's decision and challenge to the validity of a traffic regulation order.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; adjudicator made no error of law; statutory scheme lawful and not discriminatory; costs assessed at £850 rather than the £1,378.60 claimed.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator's parking decision may be challenged only on error of law and within time; a Blue Badge does not exempt a driver from residents' permit requirements where the scheme lawfully balances resident and disabled parking needs; parking adjudicator procedures treat all citizens alike and comply with Article 6; challenge to a traffic regulation order under Schedule 9 paragraph 35 must be brought within six weeks.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in law in dismissing the parking appeal
Whether the traffic regulation order unlawfully discriminated against disabled persons
Whether adjudicator procedures breached Articles 6 and 14 ECHR
Whether a medical member was required on the adjudicator panel

enrichment.short_title: ECJ reference expedition and intervener costs in airline compensation challenge
key_facts: IATA and ELFAA brought judicial review challenging the validity of EC Regulation 261/2004 on passenger compensation, due to take effect in February 2005.
The court decided to make an Article 234 EC reference and heard whether to request priority or exceptional urgency from the ECJ President.
ERA and ADL sought permission to file evidence on proportionality and airline viability risks.
Evidence suggested airlines faced liabilities that could wipe out profits and criminal penalties would apply for non-compliance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary application in consolidated judicial review proceedings for ECJ reference terms, expedition, and permission for third-party evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference to be made; court outlined grounds capable of supporting exceptional urgency under Articles 55 and 104A; ERA and ADL permitted to file evidence but ordered to bear their own costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where airline operators face serious viability risks from imminent invalid legislation carrying criminal penalties and a strong Article 251 argument exists, a national court may properly request ECJ expedition; commercial entities who voluntarily intervene to influence proceedings without becoming parties should ordinarily bear their own costs rather than expose the government department to additional costs risk.
legal_issues: Whether the court should request ECJ priority or exceptional urgency
Whether ERA and ADL should be permitted to file evidence
What costs order should apply to non-party interveners
Whether IATA's offer to adopt the evidence altered the costs position

enrichment.short_title: Whether without-prejudice letter acknowledged debt under Limitation Act
key_facts: Ross claimed about £83,000 from McGrath for building materials, loans, and related business dealings from 1990-1991.
The claim was issued in April 2002, more than six years after the causes of action accrued.
McGrath wrote a 1 May 1996 letter marked without prejudice confirming willingness to pay specified amounts when funds were available.
Grigson J held the letter was not privileged and amounted to an acknowledgment extending limitation; McGrath appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from determination of a preliminary issue on whether a 1996 letter acknowledged indebtedness within sections 29 and 30 of the Limitation Act 1980.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; letter held to acknowledge liability under each debt head while reserving position on exact amounts; respondent's costs summarily assessed at £7,168.68.
enrichment.ratio: An acknowledgment under section 29(5) must admit indebtedness and legal liability, need not state the precise amount if ascertainable by extrinsic evidence, and must be construed as a whole in context; a letter confirming willingness to pay specified sums listed in response to draft acknowledgment requests acknowledges the claims even where marked without prejudice and phrased as confirming amounts the creditor suggested.
legal_issues: Whether the 1 May 1996 letter amounted to an acknowledgment under section 29(5)
How the without prejudice marking affected admissibility
Whether the letter acknowledged all claimed debts or only reserved on amounts
Whether extrinsic evidence could identify the acknowledged debts

Dungate v Dungate [1965] 1 WLR 1477

enrichment.short_title: Refusal of permission to appeal on EC competition causation
key_facts: Arkin, assignee of BCL Shipping Line, sued shipping conference members for alleged Article 81 and 82 breaches on North Continent-Israel routes from April 1991.
After a 50-day trial Colman J dismissed the claim, holding no breaches and that BCL irrationally remained in a loss-making rate war when a reasonable trader would have exited.
Pre-April 1991 conduct was time-barred, so only post-limitation losses were recoverable if causation was established.
The action was largely funded by MPC; Arkin was impecunious and sought a stay of the costs order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal Colman J's judgment, with adjourned argument on causation and whether terms should be imposed.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no reasonable prospect of overturning finding that BCL's irrational conduct broke the chain of causation; remittal for damages on a different basis would be unjust.
enrichment.ratio: Where pre-limitation competition breaches are barred, a claimant must prove separate post-limitation damage; if by April 1991 a rational trader would have withdrawn from the market, continuing losses are attributable to the claimant's own unreasonable conduct rather than the defendant's breach; an impecunious assignee cannot at a late stage reshape the claim to pursue modest exclusion damages unsupported by evidence.
legal_issues: Whether there was a reasonable prospect of success on causation
Whether BCL acted unreasonably by remaining in the market after April 1991
Whether limitation should restrict the court to a hypothetical post-April 1991 market
Whether the case should be remitted for assessment of damages on a different basis
linked_authorities: Galoo Ltd v Bright Grahame Murray [1994] 1 WLR 1360
FMC (European competition mitigation authority)

enrichment.short_title: Indefinite all proceedings order against vexatious litigant
key_facts: Since 1995 Mr Burgess had instituted numerous private prosecutions, civil claims, and judicial reviews against police, local authorities, landlords, and lawyers.
Multiple sets of proceedings were struck out, dismissed, or treated as abandoned; judges described him as obsessed with litigation.
An interim section 42 order had been in place since February 2001 pending medical evidence of fitness to litigate.
Mr Burgess failed to comply with an unless order requiring acceptable medical evidence or consent to examination by May 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application for a final all proceedings order under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 after an interim order and unless order.
enrichment.outcome: Indefinite all proceedings order made; court satisfied Burgess habitually and persistently instituted vexatious civil and criminal proceedings without reasonable ground and had been given opportunity to be heard.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 42, where a person habitually and persistently institutes vexatious proceedings with little legal basis causing disproportionate inconvenience and expense, an all proceedings order of indefinite duration may be made if no lesser measure will prevent continuing abuse; the civil standard of proof applies; vexatious proceedings are those with no discernible legal basis that abuse court process.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Burgess habitually and persistently instituted vexatious proceedings
Whether he had a reasonable ground for the litigation
Whether an all proceedings order rather than a lesser order was necessary
Whether adequate notice and opportunity to be heard had been given
linked_authorities: AG v Barker [2001] 1 FLR 259
AG v Hayward (1995) The Times, 20 November 1995

confidence.notes: Order made and statutory test applied with extensive chronology. Medical fitness was not finally litigated due to non-compliance.

enrichment.short_title: Quashing stay of VAT fraud prosecution for non-justiciability
key_facts: Customs prosecuted Theobald, financial director of European Cellular Trading, for conspiracy to defraud the Revenue of about £14m through VAT carousel fraud on mobile phones.
Customs came into possession of Theobald's legally privileged solicitor attendance note and derivative investigative material.
At committal the District Judge stayed proceedings as an abuse on non-justiciability grounds after neither party called evidence beyond a section 10 admission of possession.
The judge found no impropriety in Customs obtaining the note but held prejudice could not be assessed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Customs' judicial review of a magistrates' court decision staying committal proceedings as an abuse of process.
enrichment.outcome: Stay quashed; voluntary bill of indictment to be served within seven days with written observations permitted; no order as to costs; renewed section 76 application dismissed as moot.
enrichment.ratio: Committal justices have a sparingly exercised abuse jurisdiction confined to fairness of trial for the accused; where a prosecutor holds privileged material, failure to explain how it was obtained and used may support an abuse argument, but a stay based on non-justiciability requires more than neutral evidence of possession and cannot rely unduly on distinguishable covert-surveillance authority when no impropriety is found; tactical failure to call evidence does not justify a non-justiciable prejudice finding.
legal_issues: Whether committal justices had jurisdiction to stay for abuse of process
Whether the judge wrongly denied Customs a half-time submission
Whether the stay for non-justiciability was Wednesbury unreasonable
What relief should follow quashing of the stay

enrichment.short_title: Protection from Eviction Act excluded licence in homeless hostel
key_facts: Rogerson and his partner were placed in a Wigan homeless persons unit flat under section 188 pending housing enquiries.
The council later accepted a section 193 duty to house them but they remained in the flat, which could be shared with strangers under the licence.
They were evicted without court order after seven days' notice following alleged licence breaches.
The unit comprised self-contained two-bedroom flats in a block with a resident warden and shared hostel rules.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Wigan County Court dismissing a claim for unlawful eviction and damages under the Protection from Eviction Act 1977.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; accommodation was in an excluded hostel licence within section 3A(8) despite also constituting the occupier's dwelling by the time notice was given.
enrichment.ratio: Accommodation is not separate and self-contained within section 622 of the Housing Act 1985 if occupiers may be required to share facilities with strangers; such enforced sharing brings premises within the excluded hostel licence under section 3A(8) of the Protection from Eviction Act 1977; even where interim homeless accommodation becomes the occupier's dwelling over time, the hostel exclusion may still defeat PEA protection.
legal_issues: Whether the premises were a hostel within section 622 Housing Act 1985
Whether the licence was an excluded licence under section 3A(8) PEA 1977
Whether the accommodation was occupied as a dwelling under section 3(2B)
Whether Mohammed v Manek prevented PEA protection after section 193 acceptance

enrichment.short_title: Assignment of hybrid personal break clause under section 63
key_facts: Midland Bank granted HSBC subsidiary Stafford a lease of Harbour Exchange floors with a break clause personal to Stafford but assignable to permitted group company assignees.
Stafford assigned the lease to parent HSBC without expressly mentioning the break clause benefit.
HSBC served notice to break on 23 June 2004; landlord Harbour Estates contended the benefit did not pass.
The break right had become valuable and both sides led evidence on rectification if automatic assignment failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated Chancery proceedings on construction of break clause assignment and alternative rectification of the 1999 assignment.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant's claim dismissed; declaration that HSBC validly exercised the break clause; counterclaim declaration granted; rectification not ordered.
enrichment.ratio: A hybrid break clause partly personal but assignable to group companies touches and concerns the lease; where assignor and assignee are group companies and the assignor had power to convey the break benefit, section 63 LPA 1925 operates to pass the benefit with an assignment of the term even without express mention, subject to the Kumar v Dunning limitation that section 63 passes only rights touching and concerning the property conveyed.
legal_issues: Whether the break clause benefit was personal or touched and concerned the land
Whether section 63 passed the break benefit with the assignment automatically
Whether section 62 or section 142 provided an alternative route of assignment
Whether rectification was required to include the break clause benefit

enrichment.short_title: Reed trade mark appeal: costs, ADR and without prejudice rule
key_facts: Following the Court of Appeal's March 2004 liability judgment in Reed Executive v Reed Business Information, parties could not agree consequential orders.
Disputes included declaration wording, ADR stay scope, interest on £350,000 interim costs payment, and allocation of costs.
Reed Employment sought disclosure of without prejudice negotiations to show RBI unreasonably refused mediation.
RBI had reduced use of the Reed name before action but Reed Employment was not told; multiple jurisdictions had parallel proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to resolve consequential orders and costs following trade mark and passing off appeal judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Without prejudice negotiations held inadmissible on costs under Walker v Wilsher; no special costs order for refusal to mediate; commercial interest rate ordered on interim payment repayment; further short hearing listed for remaining costs issues.
enrichment.ratio: The rule in Walker v Wilsher remains good law after Halsey: courts cannot order disclosure of wholly without prejudice negotiations for costs purposes unless both parties agree or Calderbank formula used; refusal to mediate late in complex multi-jurisdictional IP litigation from a position of strength is not necessarily unreasonable; commercial not judgment rate applies to repayment of interim costs payments.
legal_issues: Whether without prejudice negotiations are admissible on the question of costs
Whether RBI unreasonably refused ADR or mediation
What rate of interest applies to repayment of interim costs
What form of declaration and ADR stay wording is appropriate
